questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A block of mass $m = 4\text{ kg}$ rests on a perfectly smooth horizontal floor. Two collinear horizontal forces act on it simultaneously: $F_1 = 20\text{ N}$ directed to the right, and $F_2 = 8\text{ N}$ directed to the left. What is the magnitude of the block's acceleration?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Isolated single block of mass m = 4 kg
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame (+x pointing to the right)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Setting up the net collinear force sum Sigma F = F1 - F2 with correct signs before dividing by mass.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic algebraic computation of acceleration, not bare formula recall.

A.diagnostic: Correctly subtracted opposing forces (20 - 8 = 12 N) and evaluated a = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s².

B.diagnostic: Scalar addition trap: added opposing forces (20 + 8 = 28 N) yielding a = 28 / 4 = 7 m/s².

C.diagnostic: Neglected opposing force F2: evaluated a = 20 / 4 = 5 m/s².

D.diagnostic: Evaluated a = F2 / m = 8 / 4 = 2 m/s² ignoring the primary driving force.

progressive_hints.title: System & Direction Selection
progressive_hints.text: Choose the positive x-axis pointing to the right. Express each force as a signed vector.

progressive_hints.title: Net Force Evaluation
progressive_hints.text: The forces act in opposite directions, so the net horizontal force is $\Sigma F_x = F_1 - F_2 = 20 - 8 = 12\text{ N}$.

progressive_hints.title: Acceleration Calculation
progressive_hints.text: Apply Newton's 2nd Law: $a = \frac{\Sigma F_x}{m} = \frac{12\text{ N}}{4\text{ kg}} = 3\text{ m/s}^2$ directed to the right.

derivation_steps: Declare positive direction along the rightward axis: $\vec{F}_1 = +20\hat{i}\text{ N}$, $\vec{F}_2 = -8\hat{i}\text{ N}$.
Net horizontal force: $\Sigma \vec{F} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 = (20 - 8)\hat{i} = +12\hat{i}\text{ N}$.
By Newton's 2nd Law, $\vec{a} = \frac{\Sigma \vec{F}}{m} = \frac{12\hat{i}\text{ N}}{4\text{ kg}} = 3\hat{i}\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A textbook of mass $m$ rests quietly on a horizontal wooden table. The Earth exerts a downward gravitational force $\vec{W} = m\vec{g}$ on the book. According to Newton's 3rd Law, which force is the exact action-reaction partner to this gravitational force?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Earth-Book interacting two-body system
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial frame fixed to Earth center

options.A: The upward gravitational force exerted by the book on the Earth
options.B: The upward normal contact force exerted by the table on the book
options.C: The downward contact force exerted by the book on the table
options.D: The frictional force between the book cover and the table surface

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Distinguishing Newton 3rd Law mutual interaction pairs from equilibrium force cancellation on a single body.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying the physical interaction agent and recipient rather than reciting definition text.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Gravitational interaction between Earth and book produces equal, opposite gravitational pull by book on Earth.

B.diagnostic: Classic trap: Normal force balances gravity on the book (Newton's 1st Law equilibrium), but is an electromagnetic contact force, not a gravitational partner.

C.diagnostic: Downward force on table is the 3rd law partner to the normal force from table on book, not to gravity.

D.diagnostic: Friction is zero for a horizontal table in static equilibrium with no tangential force.

progressive_hints.title: Interaction Partner Rule
progressive_hints.text: Newton's 3rd Law pairs must involve the SAME physical interaction type (gravitational, electromagnetic) between the SAME two bodies with roles swapped.

progressive_hints.title: Identify Agent and Object
progressive_hints.text: The force is: Body 1 (Earth) pulls Body 2 (Book) downward via gravity. Swap Body 1 and Body 2.

progressive_hints.title: Synthesize Reaction
progressive_hints.text: The reaction partner is: Body 2 (Book) pulls Body 1 (Earth) upward with equal magnitude via gravity.

derivation_steps: Newton's 3rd Law states that if body $A$ exerts a force $\vec{F}_{AB}$ on body $B$, then body $B$ exerts an equal and opposite force $\vec{F}_{BA} = -\vec{F}_{AB}$ on body $A$.
Here, $A = \text{Earth}$, $B = \text{Book}$, and the interaction mechanism is gravitation.
Therefore, the reaction partner to $\vec{F}_{\text{Earth}\to\text{Book}}^{\text{grav}}$ is strictly $\vec{F}_{\text{Book}\to\text{Earth}}^{\text{grav}}$.

limiting_cases.condition: Remove the table completely (book in free fall)
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Earth still attracts book, book still attracts Earth with equal magnitude; normal force vanishes
F_grav -> 0 and reaction force on Earth -> 0

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Which of the following groups consists exclusively of physical quantities that are vectors and whose SI base units have the dimensions $[M L T^{-1}]$ or $[M L T^{-2}]$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Kinematic & dynamic state classifications

options.B: Work, Kinetic Energy, Linear Momentum, Torque

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Strictly filtering quantities that simultaneously satisfy vector status and momentum/force dimensional constraints.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Direct factual retrieval and dimensional taxonomy check without causal narrative.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Momentum and Impulse are vectors with [M L T^-1]; Force and Weight are vectors with [M L T^-2].

B.diagnostic: Work and Kinetic Energy are scalars with dimensions [M L^2 T^-2].

C.diagnostic: Pressure is a scalar quantity (force per unit area with no unique spatial direction).

D.diagnostic: Power is a scalar quantity [M L^2 T^-3].

progressive_hints.title: Vector vs Scalar Criterion
progressive_hints.text: Recall that Work, Energy, and Power are dot products or rate of dot products, making them scalars.

progressive_hints.title: Check Pressure
progressive_hints.text: Pressure acts perpendicularly inward in all directions on an immersed surface; it is a scalar, not a vector.

progressive_hints.title: Evaluate Group A
progressive_hints.text: Momentum ($m\vec{v}$) has $[M L T^{-1}]$; Impulse ($\vec{F}\Delta t$) has $[M L T^{-1}]$; Force and Weight have $[M L T^{-2}]$. All are vectors.

derivation_steps: Linear momentum: $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ (Vector, $[M L T^{-1}]$).
Impulse: $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F} dt = \Delta \vec{p}$ (Vector, $[M L T^{-1}]$).
Force: $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ (Vector, $[M L T^{-2}]$).
Weight: $\vec{W} = m\vec{g}$ (Vector, $[M L T^{-2}]$).
model_proof.final_expression: \text{Group A contains strictly vectors with }[M L T^{-1}]\text{ and }[M L T^{-2}]

limiting_cases.condition: Inspect scalars in B, C, D
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Work in B is scalar; Pressure in C is scalar; Power in D is scalar

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A student of mass $m = 60\text{ kg}$ stands on a spring bathroom scale fixed to the floor of an elevator. The elevator accelerates downward at a constant acceleration of $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what force reading does the scale register?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Student alone as isolated free body
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with downward vertical axis positive
idealizations: Spring scale displays normal contact force N

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Setting up the vertical force balance on the student with correct acceleration sign: mg - N = ma => N = m(g - a).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires modeling the contact reading as normal force under vertical acceleration constraint.

B.diagnostic: Inverted acceleration direction: evaluated N = m(g + a) = 60(12) = 720 N (corresponds to upward acceleration).

C.diagnostic: Assumed scale always reads stationary weight mg = 600 N regardless of elevator motion.

D.diagnostic: Reported net force F_net = m*a = 120 N instead of the normal contact force N.

progressive_hints.title: Isolate the Student
progressive_hints.text: Draw the FBD of the student: downward gravity $mg = 600\text{ N}$ and upward normal force $N$ from the scale.

progressive_hints.title: Newton's 2nd Law in Downward Direction
progressive_hints.text: Since the student accelerates downward at $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$, the downward net force is $mg - N = ma$.

progressive_hints.title: Solve for Normal Force
progressive_hints.text: Rearranging gives $N = m(g - a) = 60(10 - 2) = 60 \times 8 = 480\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Isolate student of mass $m = 60\text{ kg}$. Forces: gravity $\vec{W} = -mg\hat{j}$, normal force $\vec{N} = +N\hat{j}$.
Downward acceleration: $\vec{a} = -a\hat{j} = -2\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$.
Newton's 2nd Law: $\Sigma F_y = N - mg = -ma \implies N = m(g - a)$.
Substitute values: $N = 60(10 - 2) = 60(8) = 480\text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A block of mass $m = 10\text{ kg}$ rests on a rough horizontal floor with static friction coefficient $\mu_s = 0.40$ and kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k = 0.30$. A horizontal force of $F = 30\text{ N}$ is applied to the block. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the magnitude of the frictional force exerted by the floor on the block?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Block on horizontal floor

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Verifying that applied driving force F = 30 N is strictly below maximum static friction threshold f_max = 40 N, meaning friction self-adjusts to match F.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Blind application of f = mu * N leads directly to the 40 N trap option.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Applied F = 30 N < f_max = 40 N, so block remains in static equilibrium with f_s = 30 N.

B.diagnostic: Equated static friction to mu_s * N = 0.4 * 100 = 40 N without checking whether applied force exceeds threshold.

C.diagnostic: Calculated mu_k * m * g * 10 = 300 N through dimensional scale error.

D.diagnostic: Assumed static friction is zero because the block does not move.

progressive_hints.title: Check Maximum Static Threshold
progressive_hints.text: Calculate the maximum static friction threshold: $f_{\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s m g$.

progressive_hints.title: Compare Applied Force to Threshold
progressive_hints.text: $f_{\text{max}} = 0.40 \times 10 \times 10 = 40\text{ N}$. The applied force is $F = 30\text{ N} < 40\text{ N}$.

progressive_hints.title: Static Equilibrium Invariant
progressive_hints.text: Because $F < f_{\text{max}}$, the block remains at rest. By $\Sigma F_x = 0$, static friction matches the applied force: $f_s = 30\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Normal force on horizontal floor: $N = mg = 10 \times 10 = 100\text{ N}$.
Limiting static friction threshold: $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = 0.40 \times 100 = 40\text{ N}$.
Applied horizontal force: $F = 30\text{ N}$. Since $F < f_{s,\text{max}}$, the block does not slip.
To maintain $\Sigma F_x = 0$, static friction self-adjusts: $f_s = F = 30\text{ N}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Block slips, dynamic friction f_k = mu_k * N = 30 N acts

questions.stem: In an ideal Atwood machine, two masses $m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 2\text{ kg}$ are connected by a light inextensible string passing over a light frictionless pulley. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the system?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two connected masses m1, m2 and string

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Eliminating internal string tension T between coupled FBD equations to solve for common acceleration a.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Standard Atwood configuration requires routine application of coupled linear equations.

B.diagnostic: Divided net force 10 N by m2 = 2 kg instead of total mass 5 kg.

C.diagnostic: Assumed falling mass descends in unconstrained free fall at g = 10 m/s².

D.diagnostic: Evaluated (m1 - m2) / (m1 * m2) * g = (1 / 6) * 10 = 1.67 m/s² truncated erroneously.

progressive_hints.title: Coupled Equations of Motion
progressive_hints.text: For descending mass $m_1$: $m_1 g - T = m_1 a$. For ascending mass $m_2$: $T - m_2 g = m_2 a$.

progressive_hints.title: Eliminate Tension T
progressive_hints.text: Add the two equations together: $(m_1 - m_2)g = (m_1 + m_2)a$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Acceleration
progressive_hints.text: Substitute numbers: $a = \frac{(3 - 2) \times 10}{3 + 2} = \frac{10}{5} = 2\text{ m/s}^2$.

derivation_steps: Equation for $m_1$: $m_1 g - T = m_1 a$.
Equation for $m_2$: $T - m_2 g = m_2 a$.
Sum of equations: $(m_1 - m_2)g = (m_1 + m_2)a$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A block of mass $m$ slides down a perfectly smooth ramp inclined at an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the magnitude of the block's acceleration parallel to the ramp?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Block on smooth inclined plane
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial frame with x-axis along ramp and y-axis perpendicular

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Projecting gravitational force vector mg onto the inclined coordinate axes: mg sin theta along the incline and mg cos theta perpendicular.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Decisive difficulty is correct trigonometric coordinate decomposition.

A.diagnostic: Correct: a = g * sin(30 deg) = 10 * 0.5 = 5 m/s².

B.diagnostic: Assumed unconstrained vertical free fall a = g = 10 m/s².

C.diagnostic: Swapped trigonometric components: evaluated a = g * cos(30 deg) = 5*sqrt(3) m/s².

D.diagnostic: Used tan(theta) ratio a = g / sqrt(3) erroneously.

progressive_hints.title: Coordinate Axes Alignment
progressive_hints.text: Align the x-axis parallel to the inclined plane pointing downward, and y-axis perpendicular to the plane.

progressive_hints.title: Decompose Gravity Vector
progressive_hints.text: Gravity acts vertically downward: parallel component is $mg \sin\theta$, perpendicular component is $mg \cos\theta$.

progressive_hints.title: Apply Newton's 2nd Law Along Incline
progressive_hints.text: $\Sigma F_x = mg \sin\theta = ma \implies a = g \sin\theta = 10 \sin 30^\circ = 5\text{ m/s}^2$.

derivation_steps: Incline tilt angle with horizontal is $\theta = 30^\circ$.
Perpendicular force balance: $\Sigma F_y = N - mg \cos\theta = 0 \implies N = mg \cos\theta$.
Parallel force balance: $\Sigma F_x = mg \sin\theta = ma$.
Acceleration: $a = g \sin 30^\circ = 10(0.5) = 5\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A cricket ball of mass $m = 0.15\text{ kg}$ travelling horizontally at $v_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$ is struck straight back by a batsman, leaving in the exact opposite direction at $v_2 = 25\text{ m/s}$. If the bat and ball remain in contact for $\Delta t = 0.01\text{ s}$, what is the average force exerted by the bat on the ball?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Cricket ball during impact

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Enforcing 1D vector sign reversal on initial velocity so momentum change is Delta p = m(v2 - (-v1)) rather than m(v2 - v1).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-step calculation involving impulse-momentum theorem and sign conventions.

B.diagnostic: Neglected velocity reversal: evaluated Delta p = 0.15(25 - 20) = 0.75 N*s, yielding F = 75 N.

C.diagnostic: Multiplied by Delta t instead of dividing: 6.75 * 0.01 = 0.0675 scale trap.

D.diagnostic: Used (v1 + v2)/2 = 22.5 m/s without momentum change relation.

progressive_hints.title: Impulse-Momentum Relation
progressive_hints.text: Recall that Impulse $\vec{J} = \vec{F}_{\text{avg}} \Delta t = \Delta \vec{p} = m \vec{v}_2 - m \vec{v}_1$.

progressive_hints.title: Direction and Signs
progressive_hints.text: If the initial direction is negative ($-20\text{ m/s}$), the final direction is positive ($+25\text{ m/s}$).

derivation_steps: Choose coordinate axis along rebound direction: $\vec{v}_1 = -20\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$, $\vec{v}_2 = +25\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$.
Change in linear momentum: $\Delta \vec{p} = m(\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1) = 0.15(25 - (-20))\hat{i} = 0.15(45)\hat{i} = 6.75\hat{i}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.
By Impulse-Momentum Theorem: $\vec{F}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t} = \frac{6.75\hat{i}\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}}{0.01\text{ s}} = 675\hat{i}\text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Two blocks of masses $m_1 = 4\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 2\text{ kg}$ are placed in direct contact on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal driving force of $F = 18\text{ N}$ is applied to block $m_1$, pushing both blocks forward. What is the magnitude of the contact force exerted by block $m_1$ on block $m_2$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two blocks in mutual contact

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Isolating block m2 alone to see that only the contact force N12 accelerates it: N12 = m2 * a_sys.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires deciding system boundaries (whole system to find acceleration, isolated m2 to find internal contact force).

A.diagnostic: Correct: a = 18 / 6 = 3 m/s². Contact force on m2 is N12 = m2 * a = 2 * 3 = 6 N.

B.diagnostic: Calculated force acting on m1: m1 * a = 4 * 3 = 12 N.

C.diagnostic: Assumed applied force F = 18 N is transmitted undiminished across the interface.

D.diagnostic: Divided 18 N equally between two blocks (18 / 2 = 9 N) ignoring unequal masses.

progressive_hints.title: Whole System Acceleration
progressive_hints.text: Treat both blocks as a single combined system of mass $M = m_1 + m_2 = 4 + 2 = 6\text{ kg}$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Acceleration
progressive_hints.text: The common acceleration is $a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{18\text{ N}}{6\text{ kg}} = 3\text{ m/s}^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Isolate Block 2
progressive_hints.text: The ONLY horizontal force acting on $m_2$ is the contact force $N_{12}$. By Newton's 2nd Law, $N_{12} = m_2 a = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Combined system acceleration: $a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{18}{4 + 2} = 3\text{ m/s}^2$.
Free-Body Diagram for block $m_2$: $\Sigma F_x = N_{12} = m_2 a$.
Substitute values: $N_{12} = 2\text{ kg} \times 3\text{ m/s}^2 = 6\text{ N}$.

options.B: Tension along string, Gravity downward, and outward Centrifugal force
options.C: Tension along string, Gravity downward, and forward Force of Motion

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Focuses on correct scientific representation and elimination of pseudo/fictitious forces in inertial frame.

A.diagnostic: Correct: In an inertial frame, only real physical forces (Tension and Gravity) act. Since v = 0, centripetal acceleration is zero.

B.diagnostic: Added fictitious centrifugal force to an inertial frame FBD; furthermore, v = 0 means m*v^2/R = 0 anyway.

progressive_hints.text: In an inertial frame of reference, a Free-Body Diagram must include ONLY real physical interactions with identifiable agents.

progressive_hints.title: Inspect Physical Agents
progressive_hints.text: What touches the bob? The string (Tension $\vec{T}$). What field acts on the bob? The Earth's gravity ($\vec{W} = m\vec{g}$).

progressive_hints.title: Check Centripetal Force
progressive_hints.text: Centripetal acceleration is $a_c = \frac{v^2}{R}$. At turnaround, $v = 0$, so $a_c = 0$. Tension balances $mg \cos\theta_0$.

derivation_steps: In the inertial lab frame, forces arise strictly from physical interactions: the string exerts tension $\vec{T}$ along the string toward the pivot, and the Earth exerts gravitational force $\vec{W} = m\vec{g}$ vertically downward.
Since the bob is instantaneously at rest ($v = 0$), the radial acceleration is $a_r = \frac{v^2}{L} = 0$.
Radial equation: $T - mg \cos\theta_0 = m a_r = 0 \implies T = mg \cos\theta_0$.
Tangential equation: $F_{\text{tan}} = mg \sin\theta_0 = m a_t \implies a_t = g \sin\theta_0$.

progressive_hints.text: The ONLY horizontal force accelerating top block $A$ is static friction from block $B$: $f_s = m_1 a$.

progressive_hints.title: Find Maximum Acceleration of A
progressive_hints.text: Max static friction is $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s m_1 g$. Therefore $a_{\text{max}} = \frac{\mu_s m_1 g}{m_1} = \mu_s g = 0.30 \times 10 = 3\text{ m/s}^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Apply to Combined System
progressive_hints.text: For no relative slip, both blocks accelerate together at $a_{\text{max}}$. Thus $F_{\text{max}} = (m_1 + m_2) a_{\text{max}} = (2 + 6) \times 3 = 24\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Isolate block $A$: $\Sigma F_x = f_s = m_1 a$. Maximum static friction $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N_A = \mu_s m_1 g$.
Maximum non-slip acceleration: $a_{\text{max}} = \frac{f_{s,\text{max}}}{m_1} = \mu_s g = 0.30 \times 10 = 3\text{ m/s}^2$.
Isolate combined system $(A + B)$: Since floor is frictionless, $\Sigma F_x = F = (m_1 + m_2) a$.

questions.stem: In a laboratory apparatus, block $A$ on a smooth horizontal table is connected by a light string that wraps around a light movable pulley $P$ before its end is anchored to a rigid wall. A hanging load $B$ is suspended directly from the axle of movable pulley $P$. If block $A$ has mass $m$ and hanging block $B$ has mass $M$, what is the kinematic relation between the horizontal acceleration $a_A$ of block $A$ and the vertical acceleration $a_B$ of block $B$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Block A, string, movable pulley P, and hanging load B

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Differentiating string length constraint x_A + 2 y_B = L twice with respect to time to prove a_A = 2 a_B.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal mathematical proof of geometric string invariance.

A.diagnostic: Correct: String length x_A + 2 y_B = L => d²x_A/dt² + 2 d²y_B/dt² = 0 => a_A = 2 a_B.

B.diagnostic: Assumed standard fixed pulley relationship a_A = a_B.

C.diagnostic: Inverted kinematic constraint: thought movable pulley accelerates faster than free end.

D.diagnostic: Squared the mechanical advantage ratio.

progressive_hints.title: Write String Length Equation
progressive_hints.text: Express the total length $L$ of the string in terms of coordinates: $L = x_A + 2 y_P + \text{constants}$.

progressive_hints.title: Connect Coordinates
progressive_hints.text: Notice that load $B$ is attached to the pulley axle, so $y_B = y_P$. Thus $x_A + 2 y_B = L$.

progressive_hints.title: Differentiate Twice
progressive_hints.text: Differentiating with respect to time: $\frac{d^2 x_A}{dt^2} + 2 \frac{d^2 y_B}{dt^2} = 0 \implies a_A = 2 a_B$.

derivation_steps: Let $x_A$ be the displacement of block $A$ from the table edge.
Let $y_B$ be the downward displacement of the movable pulley carrying load $B$.
The string loops around pulley $P$ and anchors at the ceiling/wall: total active string length $L = x_A + 2 y_B$.
Since the string is inextensible, $\frac{dL}{dt} = 0$ and $\frac{d^2 L}{dt^2} = 0$.
Differentiating twice: $\ddot{x}_A + 2 \ddot{y}_B = 0 \implies a_A = 2 a_B$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Each of the 2 vertical segments elongates by 1 cm, pulling 2 cm from horizontal string: Delta x_A = 2 Delta y_B

limiting_cases.condition: Movable pulley mass m_p -> 0 with zero friction
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Tension in continuous string remains uniform throughout

questions.stem: A smooth wedge with an inclined face of angle $\theta = 45^\circ$ to the horizontal is accelerated horizontally to the right across a flat table with constant acceleration $A$. A small block of mass $m$ rests on the inclined face of the wedge without any friction. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what must be the acceleration $A$ of the wedge so that the block remains stationary relative to the wedge?

system_parameters.reference_frame: Non-inertial frame of wedge accelerating at A to the right

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Balancing the fictitious pseudo force mA leftward with normal reaction and gravity: N sin theta = mA and N cos theta = mg => A = g tan theta.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires coordinating non-inertial frame dynamics or 2D vector acceleration resolution.

A.diagnostic: Correct: In wedge frame, N*sin(theta) = mA and N*cos(theta) = mg => A = g*tan(theta) = 10*tan(45) = 10 m/s².

B.diagnostic: Evaluated A = g * sin(45 deg) = 5*sqrt(2) m/s².

C.diagnostic: Evaluated A = g / cos(45 deg) = 10*sqrt(2) m/s².

D.diagnostic: Assumed acceleration is halved on 45° incline: 10 / 2 = 5 m/s².

progressive_hints.title: Choose Reference Frame
progressive_hints.text: Work in the reference frame of the wedge. Since the wedge accelerates rightward at $A$, an apparent pseudo-force $mA$ acts to the LEFT on the block.

progressive_hints.title: Set Up Balance of Forces
progressive_hints.text: The normal force $N$ acts perpendicular to the incline. Vertically: $N \cos\theta = mg$. Horizontally: $N \sin\theta = mA$.

progressive_hints.title: Divide Equations
progressive_hints.text: $\frac{N \sin\theta}{N \cos\theta} = \frac{mA}{mg} \implies \tan\theta = \frac{A}{g} \implies A = g \tan 45^\circ = 10(1) = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

derivation_steps: In the non-inertial frame of the wedge, the forces acting on the block are:
1. Real gravity: $\vec{W} = -mg\hat{j}$.
2. Real normal force: $\vec{N} = -N\sin\theta\hat{i} + N\cos\theta\hat{j}$.
3. Inertial pseudo-force: $\vec{F}_{\text{pseudo}} = -m\vec{A} = -mA(-\hat{i}) = +mA\hat{i}$ (pointing to the left).
For relative equilibrium along the incline: $N \sin\theta = mA$ and $N \cos\theta = mg$.
Dividing yields $A = g \tan\theta = 10 \tan 45^\circ = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: A -> infinity (Normal force cannot provide upward support)

questions.stem: A test rocket of mass $M_0 = 1000\text{ kg}$ is fired in deep space where external gravitational forces are negligible. Its engine ejects burnt fuel gases at a constant exhaust velocity of $u_{\text{rel}} = 1200\text{ m/s}$ relative to the rocket, at a constant rate of $r = \frac{dm}{dt} = 5.0\text{ kg/s}$. What is the magnitude of the thrust force exerted on the rocket, and what is its initial acceleration?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying Newton's 2nd Law for variable mass systems: F_thrust = u_rel * (dm/dt) and evaluating initial acceleration a0 = F_thrust / M0.

C.diagnostic: Divided by 10000 instead of 1000 kg, giving a0 = 0.60 m/s².

progressive_hints.text: Thrust arises from momentum carried away by exhaust: $F_{\text{thrust}} = u_{\text{rel}} \frac{dm}{dt}$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Thrust Force
progressive_hints.text: $F_{\text{thrust}} = 1200\text{ m/s} \times 5.0\text{ kg/s} = 6000\text{ N}$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Initial Acceleration

The reaction thrust force is $F_{\text{thrust}} = u_{\text{rel}} r = 1200\text{ m/s} \times 5.0\text{ kg/s} = 6000\text{ N}$.
Initial acceleration at $t = 0$: $a_0 = \frac{F_{\text{thrust}}}{M_0} = \frac{6000\text{ N}}{1000\text{ kg}} = 6.0\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.stem: A passenger car travels along a level highway at speed $v_0 = 72\text{ km/h} = 20\text{ m/s}$. The static friction coefficient between tyres and dry asphalt is $\mu_s = 0.80$, while the kinetic friction coefficient is $\mu_k = 0.60$. With modern Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) active, the wheels continue rolling at the verge of skidding throughout braking. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the minimum stopping distance achievable?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Automobile during non-skid emergency braking
idealizations: ABS maintains maximum static friction threshold

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Selecting static friction mu_s rather than kinetic mu_k because ABS prevents wheel locking, and coupling deceleration a = mu_s * g to kinematics v² = 2 a d.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires deciding static vs kinetic friction regime under ABS conditions and coupling with kinematics.

B.diagnostic: Used kinetic friction mu_k = 0.60 (skidding with locked wheels): a = 6 m/s², d = 400 / 12 = 33.3 m.

C.diagnostic: Omitted factor of 2 in kinematics: evaluated d = v0² / a = 400 / 8 = 50 m.

D.diagnostic: Confused speed 20 m/s with distance 20 m.

progressive_hints.title: ABS Physical Mechanism
progressive_hints.text: Anti-lock brakes prevent wheels from locking and skidding; the tyres remain in rolling contact, which utilizes STATIC friction $\mu_s$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Maximum Deceleration
progressive_hints.text: Max braking force is $f_s = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$. Acceleration is $a_{\text{max}} = \frac{\mu_s mg}{m} = \mu_s g = 0.80 \times 10 = 8.0\text{ m/s}^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Kinematic Stopping Formula
progressive_hints.text: Using $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2 a d = 0 \implies d = \frac{v_0^2}{2 a} = \frac{20^2}{2 \times 8.0} = \frac{400}{16} = 25.0\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: In non-skidding rolling braking, the contact patch is instantaneously stationary relative to the road; hence the braking force is governed by static friction $\mu_s$.
Maximum braking force: $F_{\text{brake}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s m g$.
Maximum deceleration: $a = \frac{F_{\text{brake}}}{m} = \mu_s g = 0.80 \times 10 = 8.0\text{ m/s}^2$.
From work-energy theorem / kinematics: $0 = v_0^2 - 2 a d \implies d = \frac{v_0^2}{2 \mu_s g}$.
Substitute $v_0 = 20\text{ m/s}$: $d = \frac{400}{2 \times 8.0} = 25.0\text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A conical pendulum consists of a small bob of mass $m = 0.50\text{ kg}$ suspended from a fixed point by a light string of length $L = 1.0\text{ m}$. The bob rotates at constant speed in a horizontal circle such that the string makes a steady angle $\theta = 60^\circ$ with the vertical. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the tension $T$ in the string?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Bob of conical pendulum in uniform horizontal circular motion

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling vertical force equilibrium T * cos(theta) = mg to determine tension directly, without requiring circular speed computation.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying that vertical equilibrium holds independently of horizontal centripetal acceleration.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Vertical equilibrium requires T * cos(60 deg) = mg => T = 5.0 / 0.5 = 10.0 N.

B.diagnostic: Equated tension to weight mg = 0.5 * 10 = 5.0 N ignoring tilt angle.

C.diagnostic: Calculated horizontal component T * sin(60 deg) = 10 * 0.866 = 8.66 N.

D.diagnostic: Used 1 / (1 - cos(60)) ratio.

progressive_hints.title: Check Vertical Acceleration
progressive_hints.text: The circle is strictly horizontal, so the bob has ZERO vertical acceleration ($a_y = 0$).

progressive_hints.title: Vertical Force Balance
progressive_hints.text: The upward component of tension must exactly balance gravity: $T \cos\theta = mg$.

derivation_steps: In the inertial lab frame, the forces acting on the bob are tension $\vec{T}$ along the string and downward weight $\vec{W} = -mg\hat{j}$.
Since the circular path is horizontal, the vertical acceleration $a_y = 0$.
Vertical force equation: $\Sigma F_y = T \cos\theta - mg = 0 \implies T = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$.
Substitute given values: $T = \frac{0.50 \times 10}{\cos 60^\circ} = \frac{5.0}{0.50} = 10.0\text{ N}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: T -> infinity (impossible to rotate in horizontal circle without vertical sag)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Three blocks $A, B, C$ of masses $m_A = 1.0\text{ kg}$, $m_B = 2.0\text{ kg}$, and $m_C = 3.0\text{ kg}$ are stacked vertically ($A$ on top of $B$, $B$ on top of $C$) on the floor of an elevator. The elevator accelerates vertically upward at $a = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the magnitude of the contact force exerted by block $B$ on block $C$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Blocks A and B as combined system resting on C

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Isolating the composite subsystem (A + B) resting on block C and calculating N_BC = (mA + mB)(g + a).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying composite boundary (A+B) and synthesizing with accelerating frame dynamics.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Block C supports both A and B. Total mass above interface = 1 + 2 = 3 kg. Effective g = g + a = 12 m/s². N_BC = 3 * 12 = 36 N.

B.diagnostic: Included mass B alone: evaluated N = mB * (g + a) = 2 * 12 = 24 N, neglecting mass A above it.

C.diagnostic: Ignored elevator acceleration: evaluated static weight (mA + mB) * g = 3 * 10 = 30 N.

D.diagnostic: Included block C as well: (1 + 2 + 3) * 12 = 72 N (force exerted by elevator floor on C, not B on C).

progressive_hints.title: System Boundary Above Interface
progressive_hints.text: The interface between $B$ and $C$ supports everything above it: both block $A$ and block $B$.

progressive_hints.title: Combined Mass
progressive_hints.text: $M_{\text{above}} = m_A + m_B = 1.0 + 2.0 = 3.0\text{ kg}$.

progressive_hints.title: Upward Acceleration Dynamics
progressive_hints.text: $N_{BC} - M_{\text{above}} g = M_{\text{above}} a \implies N_{BC} = M_{\text{above}}(g + a) = 3.0(10 + 2) = 36.0\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Isolate the two-block composite subsystem consisting of blocks $A$ and $B$.
Total mass of subsystem: $M = m_A + m_B = 1.0 + 2.0 = 3.0\text{ kg}$.
External forces on this subsystem: downward gravitational weight $W = M g$, upward normal force from block $C$ denoted $N_{BC}$.
Newton's 2nd Law for upward accelerating subsystem: $\Sigma F_y = N_{BC} - M g = M a$.
Solve for $N_{BC}$: $N_{BC} = M(g + a) = 3.0\text{ kg} \times (10 + 2.0)\text{ m/s}^2 = 3.0 \times 12.0 = 36.0\text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A block of mass $M = 4.0\text{ kg}$ on a rough horizontal tabletop with coefficient of static friction $\mu = 0.25$ is connected by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging mass $m = 2.0\text{ kg}$. To prevent the system from accelerating, a rider mass $m_0$ is placed on top of block $M$. The static friction between $m_0$ and $M$ is $\mu_0 = 0.40$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the minimum rider mass $m_0$ required to keep the system in static equilibrium?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Coupled table system (M + m0) connected to hanging load m

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Deducing that table friction depends on total normal force (M + m0)g, and setting up inequality mu * (M + m0) * g >= m * g to solve for m0.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Synthesizes multi-body equilibrium, normal force transfer across stacked blocks, and string tension.

A.diagnostic: Correct: To prevent motion, mu * (M + m0) >= m => 0.25(4 + m0) >= 2 => 4 + m0 >= 8 => m0 >= 4.0 kg.

B.diagnostic: Set rider mass equal to hanging mass m0 = m = 2.0 kg without dividing by friction coefficient.

C.diagnostic: Calculated (M + m) / mu scale error.

D.diagnostic: Used mu0 = 0.40 on table instead of table friction mu = 0.25: 0.40(4 + m0) >= 2 => m0 = 1.0 kg.

progressive_hints.title: Equilibrium Tension
progressive_hints.text: For the hanging mass to be at rest, string tension must equal hanging weight: $T = mg = 2.0 \times 10 = 20\text{ N}$.

progressive_hints.title: Table Friction Balance
progressive_hints.text: Tension pulls block $M$ horizontally. To prevent sliding, maximum static friction at table interface must satisfy $f_{\text{max}} = \mu N_{\text{table}} \ge T$.

progressive_hints.title: Normal Force on Table
progressive_hints.text: The table supports both $M$ and $m_0$, so $N_{\text{table}} = (M + m_0)g$. Thus $0.25(4.0 + m_0)(10) \ge 20 \implies 4.0 + m_0 \ge 8.0 \implies m_0 \ge 4.0\text{ kg}$.

derivation_steps: In static equilibrium, hanging mass $m$ satisfies $T = mg$.
The horizontal force pulling on mass $M$ is string tension $T$.
The normal contact force exerted by the tabletop on block $M$ supports both blocks: $N = (M + m_0)g$.
The condition for the system to remain stationary is $f_{\text{max}} = \mu N \ge T$.
Substitute expressions: $\mu (M + m_0)g \ge mg \implies \mu (M + m_0) \ge m$.
Solve for $m_0$: $M + m_0 \ge \frac{m}{\mu} \implies m_0 \ge \frac{m}{\mu} - M = \frac{2.0}{0.25} - 4.0 = 8.0 - 4.0 = 4.0\text{ kg}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: m0 -> infinity (Impossible to prevent slip on frictionless table)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A small particle of mass $m$ is placed at the highest point of a fixed, smooth vertical circular cylinder of radius $R$. Given an infinitesimal initial nudge, the particle slides down along the frictionless cylindrical surface. At what vertical angle $\theta_c$ measured from the top vertical apex does the particle lose contact with the cylinder?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Particle sliding on smooth convex circular cylinder
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial polar frame centered at cylinder axis

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Deducing the detachment boundary condition N = 0 in radial dynamics mg cos theta - N = m v² / R, and coupling with energy conservation v² = 2 g R (1 - cos theta) to prove cos theta_c = 2/3.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal mathematical derivation of radial constraint detachment.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Radial equation mg*cos(theta) - N = m*v²/R with N = 0 gives v² = g*R*cos(theta). Energy conservation gives v² = 2*g*R*(1 - cos(theta)). Equating: cos(theta) = 2(1 - cos(theta)) => 3 cos(theta) = 2 => cos(theta_c) = 2/3.

B.diagnostic: Selected theta = 60 deg (cos = 1/2) assuming half-angle release.

C.diagnostic: Arrived at 1/3 through algebraic factor inversion.

D.diagnostic: Selected 3/4 from inverted coefficient ratio.

progressive_hints.title: Detachment Condition
progressive_hints.text: Contact is lost when the normal force drops to zero: $N = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Radial Dynamic Equation
progressive_hints.text: Along the inward radial direction toward cylinder center: $mg \cos\theta - N = \frac{m v^2}{R}$. When $N = 0$, $v^2 = g R \cos\theta$.

progressive_hints.title: Apply Conservation of Mechanical Energy
progressive_hints.text: Vertical descent is $h = R(1 - \cos\theta)$. Energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = mgh = mgR(1 - \cos\theta) \implies v^2 = 2gR(1 - \cos\theta)$. Equate $v^2$ to find $\cos\theta_c$.

derivation_steps: Let $\theta$ be the angular displacement from the topmost vertical apex.
Conservation of mechanical energy (taking apex as potential energy reference): $E = mgR = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgR\cos\theta \implies v^2 = 2gR(1 - \cos\theta)$.
Radial equation of motion toward the center of curvature: $\Sigma F_r = mg \cos\theta - N = \frac{m v^2}{R}$.
At the moment of detachment, normal contact force vanishes: $N = 0$.
Therefore, $mg \cos\theta_c = \frac{m v^2}{R} \implies v^2 = g R \cos\theta_c$.
Equating both expressions for $v^2$: $g R \cos\theta_c = 2 g R (1 - \cos\theta_c)$.
Divide by $g R$: $\cos\theta_c = 2 - 2\cos\theta_c \implies 3\cos\theta_c = 2 \implies \cos\theta_c = \frac{2}{3}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Speed at detachment v = sqrt(2/3 g R)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A wedge of mass $M$ with an inclined face of angle $\alpha$ rests on a perfectly smooth horizontal floor. A block of mass $m$ is placed on the smooth face of the wedge and released from rest. Both bodies are free to move. What is the magnitude of the horizontal acceleration $A$ of the wedge?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Wedge of mass M and block of mass m

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Formulating the coupled normal contact reaction N between wedge and block, enforcing kinematic wedge-surface contact constraint, and deriving A = mg sin alpha cos alpha / (M + m sin² alpha).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires complete deductive proof connecting multi-body constraint kinematics and dynamic normal force.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Normal force N drives wedge horizontally M*A = N*sin(alpha). Kinematic constraint gives N = m*g*cos(alpha) / (1 + (m/M)*sin²(alpha)), yielding A = m*g*sin(alpha)*cos(alpha) / (M + m*sin²(alpha)).

B.diagnostic: Neglected contact inclination projection in denominator and trigonometric coupling.

C.diagnostic: Assumed static normal reaction N = mg cos alpha without wedge recoil reduction.

D.diagnostic: Swapped sine and cosine terms in denominator.

progressive_hints.title: Horizontal Force on Wedge
progressive_hints.text: The normal force $N$ acts perpendicular to the wedge face. Its horizontal component pushes the wedge leftward: $M A = N \sin\alpha$.

progressive_hints.title: Equation of Motion for Block
progressive_hints.text: In the accelerating frame of the wedge (acceleration $A$ to the left), a pseudo-force $mA$ acts rightward on block $m$.

progressive_hints.title: Perpendicular Dynamic Balance
progressive_hints.text: Perpendicular to incline: $N = mg \cos\alpha - mA \sin\alpha$. Substitute $N = \frac{MA}{\sin\alpha}$ to solve for $A$.

derivation_steps: Let horizontal axis be positive in the direction of wedge recoil.
Horizontal equation for wedge alone: $\Sigma F_{x,\text{wedge}} = N \sin\alpha = M A \implies N = \frac{M A}{\sin\alpha}$.
Consider the block in the non-inertial frame of the wedge:
Perpendicular to the inclined face, the block remains in contact without lifting off: $\Sigma F_\perp = mg \cos\alpha - N - m A \sin\alpha = 0$.
Substitute $N = \frac{MA}{\sin\alpha}$: $mg \cos\alpha - mA \sin\alpha = \frac{M A}{\sin\alpha}$.
Multiply by $\sin\alpha$: $mg \sin\alpha \cos\alpha - m A \sin^2\alpha = M A$.
Rearrange terms: $A(M + m \sin^2\alpha) = mg \sin\alpha \cos\alpha$.
Solve for $A$: $A = \frac{m g \sin\alpha \cos\alpha}{M + m \sin^2\alpha}$.

limiting_cases.condition: alpha -> 90 deg (vertical free fall of block)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are connected by a light elastic spring of stiffness $k$. The upper mass $m_1$ is suspended from the ceiling of an elevator by an inextensible thread, while $m_2$ hangs freely from $m_1$ via the spring. The elevator is initially at rest. Suddenly, the upper supporting thread is severed. At the exact instant immediately following the cut ($t = 0^+$), what are the accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$ of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ respectively?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two masses m1 and m2 connected by spring
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with downward direction positive

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Recognizing that spring force k*x = m2*g cannot change instantaneously, so at t = 0+ m1 experiences both gravity m1*g and downward spring pull m2*g, while m2 experiences balanced forces yielding a2 = 0.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires quantitative dynamic force synthesis at instantaneous boundary discontinuity.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Spring extension x0 = m2*g / k cannot change instantaneously. On m1: F_net = m1*g + m2*g => a1 = (1 + m2/m1)g downward. On m2: F_net = m2*g - k*x0 = 0 => a2 = 0.

B.diagnostic: Treated spring as rigid rod: assumed both bodies immediately fall in free fall at g.

C.diagnostic: Assumed m1 = m2, giving a1 = 2g without retaining general mass ratio.

D.diagnostic: Omitted gravitational force on m1, taking F_net = m2*g.

progressive_hints.title: Spring Extension Continuity
progressive_hints.text: A spring has physical extension $x_0 = \frac{m_2 g}{k}$. Changing spring length requires finite time; therefore, at $t = 0^+$, the spring force is STILL $F_s = m_2 g$ upward on $m_2$ and downward on $m_1$.

progressive_hints.title: Inspect Forces on Lower Mass m2
progressive_hints.text: Gravity pulls downward with $m_2 g$; spring pulls upward with $F_s = m_2 g$. Net force on $m_2$ is $m_2 g - m_2 g = 0 \implies a_2 = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Inspect Forces on Upper Mass m1
progressive_hints.text: Both gravity ($m_1 g$) and spring tension ($m_2 g$) pull DOWNWARD on $m_1$: $F_{\text{net}} = m_1 g + m_2 g = (m_1 + m_2)g$. Thus $a_1 = \frac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1} g = \left(1 + \frac{m_2}{m_1}\right)g$.

derivation_steps: Before the thread is cut ($t = 0^-$), the system is in static equilibrium.
Equilibrium of lower mass $m_2$: $k x_0 = m_2 g \implies x_0 = \frac{m_2 g}{k}$.
Immediately after the cut ($t = 0^+$), positions and velocities cannot change discontinuously: spring extension remains $x_0$.
Forces acting on mass $m_2$ at $t = 0^+$: downward gravity $m_2 g$, upward spring tension $k x_0 = m_2 g$.
Net force on $m_2$: $\Sigma F_2 = m_2 g - k x_0 = m_2 g - m_2 g = 0 \implies a_2 = 0$.
Forces acting on mass $m_1$ at $t = 0^+$: downward gravity $m_1 g$, downward spring pull $k x_0 = m_2 g$.
Net force on $m_1$: $\Sigma F_1 = m_1 g + k x_0 = (m_1 + m_2)g$.
Acceleration of $m_1$: $a_1 = \frac{\Sigma F_1}{m_1} = \frac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1} g = \left(1 + \frac{m_2}{m_1}\right)g$ directed downward.

limiting_cases.condition: Center of mass acceleration: a_cm = (m1*a1 + m2*a2)/(m1 + m2) = ((m1 + m2)g + 0)/(m1 + m2) = g
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Matches external gravity perfectly: a_cm = g

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A heavy crate of mass $m$ rests on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of friction $\mu$. A worker pulls the crate using a rope inclined at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. To maintain uniform steady motion of the crate, what pulling angle $\theta_{\text{opt}}$ minimizes the required pulling force $F$, and what is the magnitude of this minimum force $F_{\text{min}}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Crate on rough floor pulled at angle theta

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Formulating force balance F cos theta = mu (mg - F sin theta) => F = mu mg / (cos theta + mu sin theta), and finding the trigonometric extremum via Cauchy-Schwarz / derivative.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires deductive calculus or Cauchy-Schwarz trigonometric optimization.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Equilibrium gives F = mu*mg / (cos theta + mu*sin theta). Denominator maximizes at tan theta = mu with maximum value sqrt(1 + mu²). Thus F_min = mu*mg / sqrt(1 + mu²).

B.diagnostic: Assumed optimal angle is always 45° regardless of friction coefficient.

C.diagnostic: Assumed pulling horizontally (theta = 0) is optimal, ignoring upward normal reduction.

D.diagnostic: Inverted angle condition to theta = arctan(1/mu).

progressive_hints.title: Normal Force Reduction
progressive_hints.text: Pulling upward at angle $\theta$ helps in two ways: $F \cos\theta$ drives the block forward, while $F \sin\theta$ lifts the block, reducing normal force to $N = mg - F \sin\theta$.

progressive_hints.title: Express F as a Function of theta
progressive_hints.text: For steady motion: $F \cos\theta = f = \mu N = \mu(mg - F \sin\theta) \implies F(\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta) = \mu mg \implies F(\theta) = \frac{\mu mg}{\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta}$.

progressive_hints.title: Maximize the Denominator
progressive_hints.text: To minimize $F$, maximize $D(\theta) = \cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 + \mu^2} \cos(\theta - \phi)$, where $\tan\phi = \mu$. The maximum is $\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}$ when $\theta = \phi = \arctan\mu$.

derivation_steps: Horizontal equilibrium: $\Sigma F_x = F \cos\theta - f = 0 \implies F \cos\theta = f$.
Vertical equilibrium: $\Sigma F_y = N + F \sin\theta - mg = 0 \implies N = mg - F \sin\theta$.
Friction relation: $f = \mu N = \mu (mg - F \sin\theta)$.
Substitute $f$: $F \cos\theta = \mu mg - \mu F \sin\theta \implies F(\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta) = \mu mg$.
Thus $F(\theta) = \frac{\mu mg}{\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta}$.
To minimize $F(\theta)$, we maximize the denominator $g(\theta) = \cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta$.
Setting derivative to zero: $g'(\theta) = -\sin\theta + \mu \cos\theta = 0 \implies \tan\theta = \mu \implies \theta_{\text{opt}} = \arctan\mu$.
At this angle: $\sin\theta = \frac{\mu}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}}$ and $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}}$.
Maximum denominator: $g_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}} + \frac{\mu^2}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}} = \frac{1 + \mu^2}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}} = \sqrt{1 + \mu^2}$.
Therefore, $F_{\text{min}} = \frac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: theta_opt -> 90 deg (pulling straight up), F_min -> mg (just lifting the crate)
